beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The first chapter uses that setting to make reciprocity physically intelligible.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The frightening feature is appetite that has lost its relation to other lives.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book then asks what changes when institutions reward the fastest consumer.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A restrained participant may lose position even while restraint would help the group.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The problem moves from private character toward the rules selecting public behavior.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A second image comes from the Greek story of Erysichthon and the sacred grove.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The chapter focuses on a boundary crossed before insatiable hunger takes command.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its useful distinction separates what can be done from what is permitted.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A resource may be accessible without every available use being acceptable.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The author extends the question to many actors making individually reasonable decisions.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: No single person needs to intend the cumulative damage those decisions produce.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The story becomes an entry into examining how refusal loses its authority.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The hungry ghost introduces a different problem from simply lacking enough food.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Consumption itself may fail to complete the act of satisfaction.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book distinguishes useful aspiration from craving that continually recreates dissatisfaction.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Learning, care and escape from deprivation still require desires worth pursuing.
